latin.647: EXCIPITUR: Manducationem Oralem corporis esse dicique supernaturalem & cælestem, non respectu organi, seu oris, quod omnino naturale sit, sed respectu modi manducandi, imprimis vero ratione Fundamenti Unionis Sacramentalis. §. IX.
latin.648: RESPON. (1) Organon manducationis, omnium maximè, ad modum Manducationis definiendum, facere; Quandoquidem Manducatio in Casu recto actionem dicit per organum seu Instrumentum, aliud aliudque, quô peragitur, modaliter diversam evasuram; Ita ipsis Lutheranis, Spiritualis & Sacramentalis Manducatio, alium aliumque modum Manducationis inferunt, non adeo ob diversitatem sui Objecti, vel Fundamenti, quod in utraque Manducatione, saltem inadæquate, idem est, scil. Corpus Christi, & Spiritualiter, & Sacramentaliter, seu Oraliter, in S. Cœna, juxta ipsos, manducandum; sed ob diversitatem Organi, quòd Spiritualis Manducatio Corporis Christi, Ore animæ spirituali, h. e. fide verâ vivâque, Sacramentalis vice versâ, Ore Corporis corporali peragatur; Hinc etiam solum naturale Organon, quô Manducatio Corporis Christi, Supernaturalis dicta, conceditur peragi, puta os Corporis Naturale, Supernaturalitati Manducationis in tantum sanè detrahit, ut non merè Supernaturalis, sed justô etiam titulô, eatenus Naturalis dici debeat, quatenus Organô Corporis naturali instituitur: At, quô respectu Manducatio audit Naturalis, eodem & Carnalis, & Capernaitica, saltem ex parte evadit, quia Capernaitæ Corpus Christi Ore quoque Corporis præsumebant manducandum; quin talis, ex potissimâ sui parte, si non ex toto, enascitur, quia Capernaitæ Manducationi suæ Orali corporis Christi, nullibi Lacerationem dentium & dejectionem cibi in Ventriculum, magis quàm ipsi Lutherani intrusisse leguntur. Quanquam utraque actio, tàm Masticatio dentium, quàm Dejectio esculenti in ventriculum, ad Manducationem hominis stricte sic dictam Oralem, & pro Objecto solidum cibum, (qualis humanum Christi corpus est) habentem, essentialiter pertineat, nec Instantiæ Autoris aliud evincant, à janua omnes totôque cœlô aberrantes. Vide supra §. I.
latin.649: Cæterùm Reformati, sicuti Mand. corp. Christi Oralem, quà Veritatem, meritò impugnant, ita adhuc magis, quà affictam eidem fidei Christianæ Fundamentalitatem. Ipsum hoc cùm & ego in Tractatulo meo Irenico facere instituissem, rationes etiam pro Fundamentalitate Oralis Manducationis ab Autore, in Anti-Irenico quodam Scripto, excogitatas, diluissem, Autor & meas rationes evertere, & suas ab exceptionibus vindicare omni ope annititur. Ab eo, hoc nomine, Paragraphis XI. XIII. ad XXIII. inclusive, in medium adducta, pro angustioribus Annotationis nostræ cancellis, tantò concisiùs perstringere nobis animus est, quantò ex allatis ab eodem persuasi firmiùs sumus, non tàm disputare eum seriò, quàm Respondentem suum instruere voluisse, quô pactô veritati etiam clarissimæ quandoque obstrepere, quóve Contradictionis velô eandem involvere atque obducere haud adeo multùm verecundandum sit, si quando id ex usu hypotheseos cujusdam antiquioris, Disputanti, fideique suæ sociis receptæ, advertitur futurum.
latin.650: Itaque mea prius enervaturus Autor, quibus perhibueram, Negationem Oralis Manducationis Corporis Christi, tam absolutam, quàm ad indignos relatam, haud lædere fundamentum fidei, etiamsi à verô aberrare, & affirmatio opposita, Spiritûs S. menti vicinior esse, concedatur; dicit (1) Non exigui momenti rem esse, Doctrinam in Scriptura clare & perspicuè propositam, vocare in dubium & fidem verbis Christi detrahere, de toto sympeplegmenô pronunciantis: Edite, bibite, hoc est Corpus meum. (2) Eum qui negat Oralem Corporis Christi Manducationem, etiam negare veram & Substantialem præsentiam ejusdem in Cœna. (3) Eundem negare Manducationem Sacramentalem, nec ullum inter Manducationem Spiritualem & Sacramentalem discrimen reliquum facere §. XI.
latin.651: Cui Resp. ad primum: Tùm Elenchô duplici, tùm duplici principii Petitione laborare. Elenchô quidem duplici: Neque enim disceptatur, vel de eo; Utrum res magni momenti sit, nec ne, Doctrinam in Scriptura clarè & perspicuè propositam, vocare in dubium itemque, verbis Christi fidem detrahere, quod est Christum facere mendacem, eóque se maximi momenti peccato implicare; Nec: Utrum Oralis Manducatio magni momenti sit, nec ne? quæ si vera, veritate Divinâ, i. e. Veritate à DEO manifestatâ, à Christo ipso indicta, non potest non eô ipsô magni momenti esse; sed de eo solummodò nunc dispicitur: Utrum, datâ Oralis Manducationis Veritate, etiam Divinâ, eóque magni momenti, tanti ista momenti sit, ut negata, fundamentum Christianæ Religionis concutiatur: vel, ut clarius loquar, dogma negetur, ipsius DEI Christique judicio, ad salutem consequendam absolutè necessarium? Itemque, negetur tale Dogma, quod uti sejungit negantem à DEO Christóque, ita communione Sanctorum ecclesiasticâ excludit? Non minùs verò duplici petitione principii Primum laborat: In quæstione enim est quam maximè: (1) Oralem Corporis Christi Manducationem esse Doctrinam clarè & perspicuè in Scriptura propositam; quandoquidem nullibi proposita legitur. Certe in Institutionis S. Cœnæ verbis hisce: Edite, hoc est Corpus meum, non clariùs proposita est, quàm in Verbis Christi Joh. 6. Nisi quis comederit Carnem Filii hominis, non habet vitam in se, in quibus tamen eam proponi, ipsimet Lutherani inficiantur. (2) Christum de toto sympeplegmenô, seu Complexo ex pane & Corpore, pronunciasse: Edite hoc est Corpus meum; cùm tale Complexum nunquam exstiterit, nec exstiturum unquam sit; Pronunciaverit verò Christus de pane, in manus accepto, benedicto, fracto, Discipulorum manibus tradito: Hoc est Corpus meum, eodem prorsus pronunciandi modo, quo paulò post pronunciabat: Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum in sanguine meo, i. e. pronunciandi modo tropicô seu figuratô, qui tamen non tollat præsentiam Corporis Christi in Cœna verissimam, Spiritualem interim admittat tantùm, utpote spirituali duntaxat, non aliô, modô manducari injuncti Joh. 6. uti inconfesso est.
latin.652: Ad Secundum & Tertium responsione unâ eâdemque defungi mihi licet, utrumque scil. Consequentia deficere: Enimverò (1) À negatione Oralis Manducationis Corporis Christi, quis unquam ad negationem Præsentiæ Corporis ejus in Cœna substantialis, progressum molietur? Quid fiet de Manducatione Spirituali non Sacramentali Joh. 6. quâ tamen mediante, Christus totus ita nobis præsens est, ut habitet in Cordibus nostris Gal. 3? Quorsum evadet omnipræsentia Corporis Christi, quandocunque Orali Manducatione, seu Sacramenti Eucharistici usu, abstinemus? Quanquam ipsa omnipræsentia Corporis Christi, Manducationi ejus, i. e. Receptioni Corporis Christi in os, non unô modô inimica sit: Quî enim receperis in os, quod vi omnipræsentiæ suæ, jam tum in Ore est? Et quomodo dentibus gutturi & stomacho subduces, quod ita Ore manducasti, ut omnibus tamen manducantis Corporis partibus, eodem temporis momento præsentissimum fuerit? (2) Nec melior obveniet nexus procedenti à Negatione Oralis Manducationis, ad Negationem Sacramentalis, quandoquidem etiam Spiritualis Manducatio, Manducationis Sacramentalis pars est, eóque Luthero ipsi, nec dubito, Lutheranís omnibus, præcipua & principalis. At verò à negatâ Manducationis Sacramentalis parte minus principali, ad negatam Sacramentalem totam vel universam, hiulca dabitur consequentia. Nec est, quod metuat A. sublatum tamen sic omne inter Sacramentalem & Spiritualem Manducationem, discrimen esse, si Oralis Corporis Christi Manducatio, S. Cœnâ exulet: Nam Sacramentalis Manducatio, à Spirituali, hôc evidenti discrimine, in perpetuum distat, ut Spiritualis nuda sit panisque manducatione destituatur; Sacramentalis verò hac panis manducatione semper gaudeat, ceu essentialiter sibi competente, Spiritualis nunquam Oralis sit, nisi in Sacramento Cœnæ; Sit verò tùm Oralis, benedicti tantùm panis, non Corporis Christi; Sacramentalis vice versâ, semper Oralis existat, panis scil. benedicti, etiam tùm cùm à spirituali Corporis Christi Manducatione sejuncta manet.

pass_a.647: It is EXCEPTED: that the Oral Eating of the body is and is called supernatural and heavenly, not in respect of the organ, or mouth, which is altogether natural, but in respect of the mode of eating, and especially by reason of the Foundation of the Sacramental Union. §. IX.
pass_a.648: REPLY. (1) That the organ of eating, most of all, makes for defining the mode of Eating; Seeing that Eating in the nominative case names an action through an organ or Instrument, one and another, by which it is performed, about to turn out modally diverse; So among the Lutherans themselves, Spiritual and Sacramental Eating import one and another mode of Eating, not so much from diversity of their Object or Foundation — which in each Eating, at least inadequately, is the same, namely Christ’s Body, to be eaten both Spiritually and Sacramentally or Oraliter in the Sacred Supper according to them — but from diversity of Organ, because Spiritual Eating of Christ’s Body is performed by the soul’s spiritual Mouth, i.e. by true living faith, and Sacramental conversely by the body’s corporal Mouth; Hence also the merely natural Organ by which the Eating of Christ’s Body called Supernatural is granted to be performed — namely the Body’s Natural mouth — so far indeed detracts from the Eating’s Supernaturality that it ought not to be called merely Supernatural, but also by just title Natural so far as it is instituted by the body’s natural Organ: But in the respect in which Eating is called Natural, in the same it also turns out Carnal and Capernaite, at least in part, because the Capernaites presumed Christ’s Body was to be eaten by the Body’s Mouth also; nay such arises from its chief part if not from the whole, because the Capernaites are nowhere read to have thrust into their Oral Eating of Christ’s body a tearing of teeth and casting of food into the Stomach more than the Lutherans themselves. Although each action, both Mastication of the teeth and Casting of the foodstuff into the stomach, essentially belongs to man’s Eating strictly so called Oral and having for Object solid food (such as Christ’s human body is), and the Author’s Instances prove nothing else — all wandering from the door and by the whole heaven. See above §. I.
pass_a.649: For the rest the Reformed, as they rightly impugn the Oral Eating of Christ’s body as to Truth, so still more as to the Fundamentalitatem affixed to it for the Christian faith. When I myself had also undertaken to do this very thing in my Irenic little Tract, and had diluted the reasons for the Fundamentalitatem of Oral Eating devised by the Author in a certain Anti-Irenic Writing, the Author strives with all force both to overturn my reasons and to vindicate his from the exceptions. What he has brought into the midst under this name in Paragraphs XI, XIII through XXIII inclusive, we mean to touch the more concisely for our Annotation’s narrower bars, the more firmly we are persuaded from what he has alleged that he wished not so much to dispute seriously as to instruct his Respondent by what pact it is not so very shameful sometimes to shout against even the clearest truth, or to wrap and cover the same with a veil of Contradiction, if ever that is noticed about to be of use to a Disputant from some older hypothesis received by him and his faith’s companions.
pass_a.650: And so the Author, about first to enervate my points by which I had held that Negation of the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body — both absolute and related to the unworthy — does not wound the foundation of faith, even if it be granted to wander from the true and the opposite affirmation to be nearer the Holy Spirit’s mind, says (1) It is no matter of slight moment to call into doubt a Doctrine clearly and perspicuously set forth in Scripture and to detract faith from Christ’s words pronouncing of the whole complex: Eat, drink, this is my Body. (2) That he who denies the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body also denies its true and Substantial presence in the Supper. (3) That the same denies Sacramental Eating and leaves no remaining distinction between Spiritual and Sacramental Eating §. XI.
pass_a.651: To which Reply to the first: It labors both with a double Elenchus and with a double Petition of the principle. With a double Elenchus indeed: For it is not disputed either about this — Whether it is a matter of great moment or not to call into doubt a Doctrine clearly and perspicuously set forth in Scripture and likewise to detract faith from Christ’s words, which is to make Christ a liar and so to involve oneself in a sin of greatest moment; Nor: Whether Oral Eating is of great moment or not? which if true, by Divine truth — i.e. Truth manifested by GOD, declared by Christ Himself — cannot but by that very fact be of great moment; but only this is now being examined: Whether, given the Truth of Oral Eating, even Divine, and so of great moment, it is of so great moment that, denied, the foundation of the Christian Religion is shaken: or, to speak more clearly, whether a dogma is denied which by GOD’s and Christ’s own judgment is absolutely necessary to obtaining salvation? And likewise, whether such a Dogma is denied which as it separates the denier from GOD and Christ, so excludes him from the Saints’ ecclesiastical communion? No less does the First labor with a double petition of the principle: For it is most of all in question: (1) That the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body is a Doctrine clearly and perspicuously set forth in Scripture — seeing it is nowhere read set forth. Certainly in these Institution words of the Sacred Supper: Eat, this is my Body, it is not more clearly set forth than in Christ’s words John 6. Unless one eats the Flesh of the Son of man, he has no life in himself — in which yet the Lutherans themselves deny that it is set forth. (2) That Christ pronounced of the whole complex, or Complex of bread and Body: Eat, this is my Body — when such a Complex never existed nor will ever exist; But Christ pronounced of the bread taken in hand, blessed, broken, handed to the Disciples’ hands: This is my Body, in altogether the same mode of pronouncing in which a little later He pronounced: This cup is the New Testament in my blood — i.e. in a tropical or figurative mode of pronouncing, which yet does not take away the most true presence of Christ’s Body in the Supper, while it admits only the Spiritual, seeing it was enjoined to be eaten only in a spiritual mode, not another, John 6 — as is uncontested.
pass_a.652: To the Second and Third I may finish with one and the same response — namely that each fails in Consequence: For (1) From negation of the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body, who will ever attempt a progress to negation of the substantial Presence of His Body in the Supper? What will become of the Spiritual non-Sacramental Eating of John 6, by which mediating yet Christ whole is so present to us that He dwells in our Hearts (Gal. 3)? Whither will the omnipresence of Christ’s Body go whenever we abstain from Oral Eating or use of the Eucharistic Sacrament? Although the very omnipresence of Christ’s Body is in more than one way hostile to His Eating — i.e. to Reception of Christ’s Body into the mouth: For how will you receive into the mouth what by the force of its omnipresence is already then in the Mouth? And how will you lead away by teeth to throat and stomach what you so ate with the Mouth that yet it was most present to all parts of the eater’s Body at the same moment of time? (2) Nor will a better nexus meet one proceeding from Negation of Oral Eating to Negation of Sacramental, seeing that Spiritual Eating also is a part of Sacramental Eating, and so for Luther himself — and I do not doubt for all Lutherans — the chief and principal. But from a denied less principal part of Sacramental Eating to the denied Sacramental whole or universal, a gaping consequence will be given. Nor is there reason for A. to fear that yet thus every distinction between Sacramental and Spiritual Eating is removed if Oral Eating of Christ’s Body is exiled from the Sacred Supper: For Sacramental Eating forever stands apart from Spiritual by this evident distinction — that Spiritual is bare and destitute of bread-eating; but Sacramental always enjoys this bread-eating as essentially belonging to it; Spiritual is never Oral except in the Supper’s Sacrament; and then it is Oral of the blessed bread only, not of Christ’s Body; Sacramental conversely always exists as Oral — namely of the blessed bread — even when it remains severed from the spiritual Eating of Christ’s Body.

647: §.IV cont.: Lutheran exception (§. IX) — Oral eating is called supernatural and heavenly not because of the mouth-organ (which is natural), but because of the mode of eating, especially the foundation of sacramental union.
648: Reply (1): the organ most of all defines the mode. Even Lutherans distinguish spiritual from sacramental eating by organ — soul’s mouth (living faith) vs body’s mouth — not by a different object (Christ’s body in both).

A natural mouth so far makes the so-called supernatural eating also Natural, and thus partly Carnal/Capernaite. Strict oral eating of solid food (Christ’s human body) essentially includes chewing and stomach-descent — see §.I. The Author’s instances miss the door by a whole heaven.
649: The Reformed impugn Oral not only as to truth but still more as to the Fundamentalitatem hung on it for Christian faith.

Strimesius’s Irenic tract answered the Author’s Anti-Irenic reasons for that fundamentality (§§XI, XIII–XXIII); he now touches them concisely — reading the Author less as serious dispute than as coaching a Respondent how to shout down clear truth for an older hypothesis.
650: The Author first tries to break Strimesius’s claim that denying Oral (absolute or as to the unworthy) does not wound faith’s foundation — even if Oral were nearer the Spirit’s mind.

Three charges (§. XI): (1) to doubt Oral is to doubt clear Institution words and make Christ a liar; (2) denying Oral denies true substantial presence; (3) it denies sacramental eating and erases spiritual/sacramental distinction.
651: Reply to (1): double elenchus + double petitio. The live question is not whether doubting clear Scripture or a truly divine Oral would be grave, but whether Oral — even if true — is so necessary that denying it shakes the Christian foundation / excludes from the saints’ communion.

Petitio: Oral is nowhere clearly set in Scripture — ‘Eat, this is my Body’ is no clearer for Oral than John 6, which Lutherans themselves deny teaches Oral. Nor did Christ pronounce of a bread+body complex that never exists; He spoke of the bread tropically, as of the cup as New Testament — without canceling most-true spiritual presence (Jn 6).
652: Reply to (2)–(3): consequence fails. Denying Oral does not deny substantial presence — witness spiritual non-sacramental eating (Jn 6; Christ dwelling in hearts). Omnipresence itself sits oddly with ‘receiving into the mouth what is already in the mouth.’

Nor does denying Oral deny sacramental eating: spiritual is the chief part of sacramental for Luther; denying a lesser part is not denying the whole. Distinction remains — spiritual bare of bread; sacramental always has blessed-bread oral, even when severed from spiritual eating of the Body. Stop mid-§.IV before §.6 / further Anti-Irenicum.

notes.647: Exception: Oral supernatural by mode/union not organ.
notes.648: Organ defines mode; natural mouth → Capernaite.
notes.651: Reply to first: elenchus + petitio; not clear in Scripture.
notes.652: Reply to 2–3: presence/sacramental remain; mid-§.IV stop.
